claim: Vision under starlight requires rod photoreceptors to transduce and transmit single-photon responses to the visual system.
source: Vision under starlight requires rod photoreceptors to transduce and transmit single-photon responses to the visual system.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about rod photoreceptor function in low-light vision.

claim: At the resting membrane potential in darkness, mouse rods exhibit coordinated and regularly timed multivesicular release events, each consisting of ~17 vesicles.
source: At the resting membrane potential in darkness, mouse rods exhibit coordinated and regularly timed multivesicular release events, each consisting of ~17 vesicles and occurring two to three times more regularly than predicted by Poisson statistics.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of glutamate transporter currents from mouse rods presented in the manuscript.

claim: Multivesicular release events occur two to three times more regularly than predicted by Poisson statistics.
source: At the resting membrane potential in darkness, mouse rods exhibit coordinated and regularly timed multivesicular release events, each consisting of ~17 vesicles and occurring two to three times more regularly than predicted by Poisson statistics.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of interevent intervals compared to Poisson predictions.

claim: Hyperpolarizing rods to mimic the voltage change produced by a single photon abruptly reduced the probability of multivesicular release nearly to zero.
source: Hyperpolarizing rods to mimic the voltage change produced by a single photon abruptly reduced the probability of multivesicular release nearly to zero with a rebound increase at stimulus offset.
evidence: This is supported by voltage-clamp experiments where simulated single-photon voltage waveforms were applied.

claim: There is a rebound increase in multivesicular release at stimulus offset following hyperpolarization.
source: Hyperpolarizing rods to mimic the voltage change produced by a single photon abruptly reduced the probability of multivesicular release nearly to zero with a rebound increase at stimulus offset.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data showing release dynamics during and after voltage stimuli.

claim: Regularly timed, multivesicular release promotes transmission of single-photon responses to post-synaptic rod-bipolar cells.
source: Simulations of these release dynamics indicate that this regularly timed, multivesicular release promotes transmission of single-photon responses to post-synaptic rod-bipolar cells.
evidence: This is based on computational simulations and ideal observer analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The multivesicular release mechanism is efficient, requiring lower overall release rates than uniquantal release governed by Poisson statistics.
source: Furthermore, the mechanism is efficient, requiring lower overall release rates than uniquantal release governed by Poisson statistics.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative modeling of different release strategies.

claim: Humans can detect flashes consisting of a few photons hitting the retina.
source: Pioneering psychophysical studies showed that humans can detect flashes consisting of a few photons hitting the retina, indicating that individual rods can respond to the absorption of single photons and then reliably signal these events to post-synaptic neurons (Barlow, 1956; Hecht et al., 1942; Sakitt, 1972; Tinsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to psychophysical studies.

claim: Individual rods can respond to the absorption of single photons and reliably signal these events to post-synaptic neurons.
source: Pioneering psychophysical studies showed that humans can detect flashes consisting of a few photons hitting the retina, indicating that individual rods can respond to the absorption of single photons and then reliably signal these events to post-synaptic neurons (Barlow, 1956; Hecht et al., 1942; Sakitt, 1972; Tinsley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from psychophysical studies and supported by citations.

claim: The ability of rods to respond to single photons was confirmed by electrophysiological recordings.
source: The ability of rods to respond to single photons was subsequently confirmed by electrophysiological recordings (Baylor et al., 1984; Gross et al., 2015; Reingruber et al., 2015; Rieke and Baylor, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: In darkness, rods maintain a relatively depolarized membrane potential of around −40 mV.
source: In darkness, rods maintain a relatively depolarized membrane potential of around −40 mV, and the absorption of a photon produces a small hyperpolarization, between 1 and 3.5 mV (Cangiano et al., 2012; Hornstein et al., 2005; Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The absorption of a photon produces a small hyperpolarization in rods, between 1 and 3.5 mV.
source: In darkness, rods maintain a relatively depolarized membrane potential of around −40 mV, and the absorption of a photon produces a small hyperpolarization, between 1 and 3.5 mV (Cangiano et al., 2012; Hornstein et al., 2005; Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Rods signal the absorption of a photon to post-synaptic rod-bipolar cells by decreasing the rate of glutamate release.
source: Rods signal the absorption of a photon to post-synaptic rod-bipolar cells by decreasing the rate of glutamate release.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rod signaling mechanisms.

claim: Synaptic vesicle release is an intrinsically noisy process that is typically described by Poisson statistics.
source: However, synaptic vesicle release is an intrinsically noisy process that is typically described by Poisson statistics (Malagon et al., 2016; Miki, 2019; Zhang and Peskin, 2015), posing a problem for post-synaptic bipolar cells to distinguish a genuine decrease in vesicle release caused by the absorption of a photon from a stochastic pause in vesicle release.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on vesicle release statistics.

claim: Poisson statistics of vesicle release pose a problem for post-synaptic bipolar cells to distinguish a genuine decrease in vesicle release caused by photon absorption from a stochastic pause.
source: However, synaptic vesicle release is an intrinsically noisy process that is typically described by Poisson statistics (Malagon et al., 2016; Miki, 2019; Zhang and Peskin, 2015), posing a problem for post-synaptic bipolar cells to distinguish a genuine decrease in vesicle release caused by the absorption of a photon from a stochastic pause in vesicle release.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the noisy nature of Poisson release.

claim: Under the assumption of Poisson release, a rod would need to maintain a basal release rate of ~100 vesicles/s to generate a sufficiently reliable signal to distinguish single-photon responses from stochastic variability.
source: Under the assumption of Poisson release, a rod would need to maintain a basal release rate of ~100 vesicles/s to generate a sufficiently reliable signal to distinguish single-photon responses from stochastic variability in vesicle release (Rao-Mirotznik et al., 1998; Rao et al., 1994; Schein and Ahmad, 2005; van Rossum and Smith, 1998).
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations cited from previous studies.

claim: Measurements from salamander, gecko, and mouse rods show basal release rates of only 10–20 vesicles/s.
source: Furthermore, measurements from salamander, gecko, and mouse rods show basal release rates of only 10–20 vesicles/s (Hays et al., 2020b; Sheng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental measurements.

claim: Implementing an Erlang process that releases vesicles at regular intervals would reduce the likelihood of mistaking a stochastic decrease in vesicle release for the absorption of a photon.
source: For example, implementing an Erlang process that releases vesicles at regular intervals would reduce the likelihood of mistaking a stochastic decrease in vesicle release for the absorption of a photon (Schein and Ahmad, 2005).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal cited from previous work.

claim: Erlang events are generated by accumulating a certain number of Poisson events, which reduces interevent variability to regularize release.
source: Erlang events are generated by accumulating a certain number of Poisson events, which reduces interevent variability to regularize release.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical properties of Erlang processes.

claim: Ribbons are plate-like, pre-synaptic structures that tether multiple vesicles along the surface.
source: Ribbons are plate-like, pre-synaptic structures that tether multiple vesicles along the surface and it has been suggested that delivery of vesicles down a ribbon may help to make release more regular (Schein and Ahmad, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribbon synapse structure.

claim: It has been suggested that delivery of vesicles down a ribbon may help to make release more regular.
source: Ribbons are plate-like, pre-synaptic structures that tether multiple vesicles along the surface and it has been suggested that delivery of vesicles down a ribbon may help to make release more regular (Schein and Ahmad, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from previous work.

claim: Glutamate transporters in rods are largely EAAT5.
source: The glutamate transporters in rods (largely EAAT5) are linked to an uncoupled anion conductance, so that an anion channel opens as glutamate is retrieved (Arriza et al., 1997; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on glutamate transporters.

claim: Glutamate transporters in rods are linked to an uncoupled anion conductance, so that an anion channel opens as glutamate is retrieved.
source: The glutamate transporters in rods (largely EAAT5) are linked to an uncoupled anion conductance, so that an anion channel opens as glutamate is retrieved (Arriza et al., 1997; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on transporter function.

claim: Glutamate reuptake into rods continues even after post-synaptic mGluR6 receptors in rod-bipolar cells become saturated.
source: Glutamate reuptake into rods continues even after post-synaptic mGluR6 receptors in rod-bipolar cells become saturated, suggesting that transporters are not saturated during rod release (Hasegawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental observations.

claim: Transporters are not saturated during rod release.
source: Glutamate reuptake into rods continues even after post-synaptic mGluR6 receptors in rod-bipolar cells become saturated, suggesting that transporters are not saturated during rod release (Hasegawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reuptake continues after receptor saturation.

claim: Glutamate anion currents vary linearly with glutamate levels in the synaptic cleft when transporters are not saturated.
source: In that range, glutamate anion currents (IA(glu)) vary linearly with glutamate levels in the synaptic cleft and can thus provide a pre-synaptic measure of glutamate release (Hasegawa et al., 2006; Otis and Jahr, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on transporter currents.

claim: Glutamate anion currents can provide a pre-synaptic measure of glutamate release.
source: In that range, glutamate anion currents (IA(glu)) vary linearly with glutamate levels in the synaptic cleft and can thus provide a pre-synaptic measure of glutamate release (Hasegawa et al., 2006; Otis and Jahr, 1998).
evidence: This is inferred from the linear relationship between currents and glutamate levels.

claim: Stochastic release of individual vesicles obeyed Poisson statistics when rods were voltage-clamped at −70 mV.
source: Using these techniques, we observed stochastic release of individual vesicles that obeyed Poisson statistics when rods were voltage-clamped at −70 mV.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and statistical analysis.

claim: At the typical resting membrane potential in darkness of −40 mV, release transitioned to regularly spaced multivesicular release events of ~17 vesicles apiece.
source: However, at the typical resting membrane potential in darkness of −40 mV, release transitioned to regularly spaced multivesicular release events of ~17 vesicles apiece (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations reported in a previous publication.

claim: The probability of initiating multivesicular release events was nearly abolished by a small membrane hyperpolarization similar to single-photon responses.
source: We found that the probability of initiating multivesicular release events was nearly abolished by a small membrane hyperpolarization similar to single-photon responses.
evidence: This is based on experimental voltage-clamp measurements.

claim: A model of the empirically determined, voltage-dependent vesicle release dynamics combined with an ideal observer analysis reproduced the detection sensitivity of mouse rod-bipolar cells.
source: A model of the empirically determined, voltage-dependent vesicle release dynamics combined with an ideal observer analysis reproduced the detection sensitivity of mouse rod-bipolar cells (Field and Rieke, 2002a).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and comparison to published data.

claim: Regularly timed multivesicular release events in rods can enhance post-synaptic detection of small voltage changes evoked by the absorption of individual photons.
source: These results show that regularly timed multivesicular release events in rods can enhance post-synaptic detection of small voltage changes evoked by the absorption of individual photons.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: The multivesicular release strategy achieves greater sensitivity than Poisson release while requiring fewer vesicles per second.
source: Furthermore, this strategy is efficient, achieving greater sensitivity than Poisson release while requiring fewer vesicles per second.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative modeling.

claim: Spontaneous inward currents in rods voltage-clamped at −70 mV showed a unimodal amplitude distribution suggesting they consisted entirely of uniquantal events.
source: Spontaneous inward currents in rods voltage-clamped at −70 mV showed a unimodal amplitude distribution suggesting they consisted entirely of uniquantal events (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements and amplitude distribution analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The overall rate of release increased at depolarized membrane potentials but achieved a rate at room temperature of only 4–5 vesicles/s at −40 mV.
source: The overall rate of release increased at depolarized membrane potentials but achieved a rate at room temperature of only 4–5 vesicles/s at −40 mV, similar to the membrane potential in darkness.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of release rates.

claim: Release rates and ICa were doubled by increasing the bath temperature to 35°C.
source: As shown previously, release rates and ICa were doubled by increasing the bath temperature to 35°C, attaining an average rate of ~11 v/s/ribbon at −40 mV (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements at different temperatures.

claim: At 35°C, rods attain an average release rate of ~11 v/s/ribbon at −40 mV.
source: As shown previously, release rates and ICa were doubled by increasing the bath temperature to 35°C, attaining an average rate of ~11 v/s/ribbon at −40 mV (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: Semi-regular multivesicular release events dominate release in rods held at −40 mV.
source: Accompanying this increased rate of vesicle release was a switch to more coordinated forms of release with semi-regular multivesicular release events dominating release in rods held at −40 mV (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Occasional unitary events were interspersed among multivesicular events at −40 mV.
source: Occasional unitary events were interspersed among these multivesicular events and so the overall distribution of event amplitudes measured at −40 mV was bimodal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The overall distribution of event amplitudes measured at −40 mV was bimodal.
source: Occasional unitary events were interspersed among these multivesicular events and so the overall distribution of event amplitudes measured at −40 mV was bimodal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on amplitude distribution analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Multivesicular release events involve the rapid sequential release of 10–20 vesicles triggered by Ca2+ influx.
source: As described previously (Hays et al., 2020b), multivesicular release events involved the rapid sequential release of 10–20 vesicles triggered by Ca2+ influx and derived from a pool of ribbon-associated vesicles shared with evoked release.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental characterization.

claim: Multivesicular release events are derived from a pool of ribbon-associated vesicles shared with evoked release.
source: As described previously (Hays et al., 2020b), multivesicular release events involved the rapid sequential release of 10–20 vesicles triggered by Ca2+ influx and derived from a pool of ribbon-associated vesicles shared with evoked release.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental characterization.

claim: Under conditions of low release probability, vesicle exocytosis occurs stochastically, obeying Poisson statistics.
source: It is generally accepted that under conditions of low release probability (e.g., when a neuron is hyperpolarized), vesicle exocytosis occurs stochastically, obeying Poisson statistics (Malagon et al., 2016; Miki, 2019; Zhang and Peskin, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Spontaneous release can arise from Ca2+ independent fusion events or from chance openings of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Spontaneous release can arise from Ca2+ independent fusion events or from chance openings of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cork et al., 2016; Kavalali, 2015; Kavalali, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on spontaneous release mechanisms.

claim: The persistence of spontaneous events in rods held at −70 mV, even after blocking Ca2+ channels with extracellular Cd2+ or strongly buffering intracellular Ca2+ with 10 mM BAPTA, showed evidence for Ca2+-independent release.
source: The persistence of spontaneous events in rods held at −70 mV, even after blocking Ca2+ channels with extracellular Cd2+ or strongly buffering intracellular Ca2+ with 10 mM BAPTA, showed evidence for Ca2+-independent release (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations with Ca2+ channel blockers and buffers.

claim: The frequency distributions of interevent intervals for release events detected in rods voltage-clamped at −70 mV consistently exhibited a single exponential decay as predicted for a Poisson release process.
source: The frequency distributions of interevent intervals for release events detected in rods voltage-clamped at −70 mV (e.g., Figure 2A) consistently exhibited a single exponential decay as predicted for a Poisson release process (R2 = 0.97 ± 0.04, mean ± SD, n = 9 rods; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The probability of the number of release events that occur in a 1 s interval at −70 mV was well fit using a Poisson probability distribution.
source: The probability of the number of release events that occur in a 1 s interval was also well fit using a Poisson probability distribution (Equation 6; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The Poisson fit for spontaneous events at −70 mV was robust (R2 = 0.94 ± 0.07, n = 9 rods).
source: The Poisson fit for spontaneous events was robust (R2 = 0.94 ± 0.07, n = 9 rods), and the mean number of events per second predicted from the Poisson fit, λ = 1.06 ± 0.55 (n = 9), was very close to the actual mean number of events observed in the same sample (λ = 1.0 ± 0.6, p=0.83, n = 9).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The mean number of events per second predicted from the Poisson fit (λ = 1.06 ± 0.55) was very close to the actual mean number of events observed (λ = 1.0 ± 0.6, p=0.83).
source: The Poisson fit for spontaneous events was robust (R2 = 0.94 ± 0.07, n = 9 rods), and the mean number of events per second predicted from the Poisson fit, λ = 1.06 ± 0.55 (n = 9), was very close to the actual mean number of events observed in the same sample (λ = 1.0 ± 0.6, p=0.83, n = 9).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of predicted and observed values.

claim: The rate of Ca2+-independent spontaneous release from rods at hyperpolarized membrane potentials is a Poisson process.
source: These results indicate that the rate of Ca2+-independent spontaneous release from rods at hyperpolarized membrane potentials is a Poisson process.
evidence: This is concluded from the statistical analysis of release at −70 mV.

claim: The intervals between unitary events at −40 mV were well described by a single exponential, consistent with an underlying Poisson release process.
source: Like those observed at −70 mV, the intervals between unitary events at −40 mV were well described by a single exponential (Figure 2D, filled squares, R2 = 0.90 ± 0.07, n = 9 rods), consistent with an underlying Poisson release process.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Histograms of interevent intervals for multivesicular events could not be fit by single exponentials, suggesting that multivesicular events are not released by a Poisson process.
source: However, if we treated each multivesicular event as an individual release event, histograms of interevent intervals could not be fit by single exponentials, suggesting that multivesicular events are not released by a Poisson process (Figure 2D, bars).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Single and multivesicular release events emerge independently.
source: It therefore appears that single and multivesicular release events emerge independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the different statistical properties of the two types of events.

claim: Glutamate transporter currents continue to increase even after saturation of post-synaptic mGluR6 receptors, indicating that transporters are not normally saturated during release from rods.
source: Glutamate transporter currents continue to increase even after saturation of post-synaptic mGluR6 receptors, indicating that transporters are not normally saturated during release from rods (Hasegawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: The charge transfer for each IA(glu) vesicle release event should sum linearly when transporters are not saturated.
source: This implies that the charge transfer for each IA(glu) vesicle release event should sum linearly.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-saturated state of transporters.

claim: A Poisson distribution could not describe the frequency distribution of individual vesicle release events at −40 mV.
source: A Poisson distribution could not describe the frequency distribution of individual vesicle release events counted in this way.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of release events.

claim: During each 1 s interval at −40 mV, there was either a multivesicular release event or no release event and so interevent intervals were distributed bimodally.
source: During each 1 s interval, there was either a multivesicular release event or no release event and so interevent intervals were distributed bimodally (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The frequency distribution of vesicle release at −40 mV could not be fit with a Poisson model, yielding negative R2 values.
source: The frequency distribution could not be fit with a Poisson model (Equation 6), yielding negative R2 values (−0.7 ± 0.6, n = 9) both when λ was unconstrained (λ = 2.5 in Figure 2F) and when λ was constrained to the actual mean number of events/s (λ = 11 in Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The statistics of multivesicular release were not well described by a Poisson distribution.
source: Thus, unlike unitary event statistics, the statistics of multivesicular release were not well described by a Poisson distribution.
evidence: This is concluded from the statistical analyses.

claim: Fitting the interevent intervals for multivesicular events with a Gaussian function yielded better fits (mean R2 = 0.84 ± 0.12) than fitting with an exponential function.
source: Fitting the interevent intervals for multivesicular events with a Gaussian function yielded better fits (mean R2 = 0.84 ± 0.12) than fitting with an exponential function.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing different fitting functions.

claim: Interevent intervals for multivesicular events averaged 2.34 ± 0.64 s (N = 16) with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 0.43 ± 0.09.
source: Interevent intervals averaged 2.34 ± 0.64 s (N = 16) with a coefficient of variation (CV) among these cells of 0.43 ± 0.09.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: For a Poisson distribution where variance = mean, the average mean intervals between multivesicular events predicted a CV of 0.67.
source: For a Poisson distribution where variance = mean, the average mean intervals between multivesicular events in this sample of cells predicted a CV of 0.67.
evidence: This is calculated from the properties of Poisson distributions.

claim: The intervals between multivesicular events were consistent with Erlang factors ranging from 3 to 12 and averaged k = 6.2 ± 3.12 (n = 16).
source: The intervals between multivesicular events were consistent with Erlang factors ranging from 3 to 12 and averaged k = 6.2 ± 3.12 (n = 16).
evidence: This is calculated from the CV values using the Erlang distribution formula.

claim: During dark adaptation, ribbons can increase in length in mouse rods.
source: During dark adaptation, ribbons can increase in length in mouse rods (Dembla et al., 2020) and bursts involve release from the pool of vesicles at the base of the ribbon (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bursts involve release from the pool of vesicles at the base of the ribbon.
source: During dark adaptation, ribbons can increase in length in mouse rods (Dembla et al., 2020) and bursts involve release from the pool of vesicles at the base of the ribbon (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: When holding dark-adapted rods at −40 mV, the number of vesicles in each multivesicular release event (16.7 ± 5.8, n = 7) did not differ significantly from those measured in retinas prepared in the light (17 ± 7 v/burst, n = 22, p=0.74).
source: However, when holding dark-adapted rods at −40 mV, we found that the number of vesicles in each multivesicular release event (16.7 ± 5.8, n = 7) and the intervals between multivesicular event start times (2.0 ± 0.54 s, n = 6, room temperature) did not differ significantly from those measured in retinas prepared in the light (17 ± 7 v/burst, n = 22, p=0.74, unpaired t-test; 2.3 ± 0.64 s intervals, n = 16, p=0.34, unpaired t-test) (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental measurements.

claim: The intervals between multivesicular event start times in dark-adapted rods (2.0 ± 0.54 s, n = 6) did not differ significantly from those measured in retinas prepared in the light (2.3 ± 0.64 s intervals, n = 16, p=0.34).
source: However, when holding dark-adapted rods at −40 mV, we found that the number of vesicles in each multivesicular release event (16.7 ± 5.8, n = 7) and the intervals between multivesicular event start times (2.0 ± 0.54 s, n = 6, room temperature) did not differ significantly from those measured in retinas prepared in the light (17 ± 7 v/burst, n = 22, p=0.74, unpaired t-test; 2.3 ± 0.64 s intervals, n = 16, p=0.34, unpaired t-test) (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental measurements.

claim: Recording from rods in light-adapted versus dark-adapted states did not strongly alter release statistics.
source: Thus, recording from rods in light-adapted versus dark-adapted states did not strongly alter release statistics.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of measurements in different adaptation states.

claim: Multivesicular events increased in amplitude during the first few minutes of recording as SCN− diffused into the rod from the patch pipette.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3, multivesicular events increased in amplitude during the first few minutes of recording as SCN− diffused into the rod from the patch pipette.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was a decrease in multivesicular event frequency after patch rupture, presumably due to rundown of the release mechanism.
source: There was also a decrease in multivesicular event frequency after patch rupture, presumably due to rundown of the release mechanism.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: When the intervals between multivesicular events were plotted against time after patch rupture, the slopes of the linear regressions were all significantly non-zero (n = 5 rods).
source: When the intervals between multivesicular events were plotted against time after patch rupture, the slopes of the linear regressions were all significantly non-zero (n = 5 rods, room temperature).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The y-intercept values of linear regressions of interevent intervals versus time averaged 1.23 ± 0.45 s.
source: The y-intercept values averaged 1.23 ± 0.45 s, whereas the overall mean interval between multivesicular events in this sample averaged 2.26 s ± 0.60 s (n = 5, room temperature).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The interevent intervals present at patch rupture were roughly half the overall average interval between multivesicular release events yielding approximately twice the release rate.
source: This suggests that the interevent intervals present at patch rupture were roughly half the overall average interval between multivesicular release events yielding approximately twice the release rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of y-intercept and mean interval values.

claim: Elevating the bath temperature significantly shortened release intervals, from 2.3 ± 0.64 s (N = 16) at room temperature to 1.13 ± 0.67 s (n = 5) at 35°C (p<0.0001).
source: Finally, we examine the impact of temperature. Due to more rapid rundown at higher temperatures, most of our recordings were performed at room temperature (~22°C). Elevating the bath temperature also significantly shortened release intervals, from 2.3 ± 0.64 s (N = 16) at room temperature to 1.13 ± 0.67 s (n = 5) at 35°C (p<0.0001, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental measurements at different temperatures.

claim: The spontaneous rate of multivesicular release events in darkness at physiological temperatures from intact mouse rods is approximately 2 Hz.
source: These various lines of reasoning converge on a spontaneous rate of multivesicular release events in darkness at physiological temperatures from intact mouse rods of ~2 Hz.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence accounting for rundown and temperature effects.

claim: In mouse rods, the voltage changes evoked by single-photon absorption average ~3.5 mV.
source: In mouse rods, the voltage changes evoked by single-photon absorption average ~3.5 mV (Cangiano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A small hyperpolarization from −40 to −43.5 mV consistently produced an appreciable pause in release.
source: To test the sensitivity of multivesicular release to small voltage changes, we voltage-clamped the rod at –40 mV for 30 s and then applied a hyperpolarizing step to −43.5 mV. This small hyperpolarization consistently produced an appreciable pause in release (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The average interevent intervals measured over a 30 s period at −43.5 mV (3744 ± 2243 ms, 129 intervals) were significantly longer than those measured in the same cells at −40 mV (2405 ± 1430 ms, 279 intervals, p<0.0001, n = 9 rods).
source: The average interevent intervals measured over a 30 s period at −43.5 mV (3744 ± 2243, 129 intervals) were significantly longer than those measured in the same cells at −40 mV (2405 ± 1430 ms, 279 intervals, p<0.0001, unpaired t-test, n = 9 rods).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental measurements.

claim: The interval to the first multivesicular event observed after the step to −43.5 mV was consistently greater than 1 standard deviation above the mean interevent intervals measured at −40 mV.
source: In addition, the interval to the first multivesicular event observed after the step to −43.5 mV (red triangles in Figure 4B show measurements from individual trials) was consistently greater than 1 standard deviation above the mean interevent intervals measured at −40 mV.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Single-photon responses of primate rods average only ~1 mV.
source: Single-photon responses of primate rods appear be smaller than those of mouse rods, averaging only ~1 mV (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Steps of −1 mV and −2 mV also produced appreciable pauses in multivesicular events immediately after the step.
source: We found that steps of −1 (n = 7; filled circles in Figure 4B) and −2 mV (n = 7; stars in Figure 4B) also produced appreciable pauses in multivesicular events immediately after the step.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The lengthening of release intervals could potentially improve the signaling of single-photon responses to post-synaptic bipolar cells.
source: This lengthening of release intervals could potentially improve the signaling of single-photon responses to post-synaptic bipolar cells, allowing genuine reductions in release caused by a photon to be distinguished from a stochastic fluctuation in release.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A voltage waveform mimicking single-photon responses was constructed from a two exponential function that attained a peak amplitude of 3.4 mV after 245 ms and then declined with a time constant of 2.5 s.
source: This voltage waveform was constructed from a two exponential function that attained a peak amplitude of 3.4 mV after 245 ms and then declined with a time constant of 2.5 s (Figure 5A; Cangiano et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the construction of the stimulus based on published data.

claim: Release probability declined almost to zero at the peak of the simulated light response, falling in parallel with membrane hyperpolarization (n = 1892 events from 28 rods).
source: Binning the multivesicular release events in time revealed that release probability declined almost to zero at the peak of the simulated light response, falling in parallel with membrane hyperpolarization (Figure 5B; n = 1892 events from 28 rods).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Multivesicular release rebounded with an overshoot as the membrane potential recovered, showing ~50% more events initiated during the first few hundred milliseconds after termination of the simulated light response.
source: Multivesicular release then rebounded with an overshoot as the membrane potential recovered, showing ~50% more events initiated during the first few hundred milliseconds after termination of the simulated light response (between 3000 and 4000 ms, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The voltage stimulus did not truncate multivesicular events that had started prior to the stimulus.
source: The voltage stimulus did not truncate multivesicular events that had started prior to the stimulus; events that continued during the stimulus had the same number of quanta, measured by charge transfer, as prior events (p=0.53, t-test, n = 5 rods, not shown).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The average stimulus waveform that preceded each multivesicular event consisted of a small hyperpolarizing excursion followed by a larger depolarizing excursion with a time course roughly similar to termination of a single-photon response.
source: The average stimulus waveform that preceded each multivesicular event, that is, the event triggered average (ETA) waveform, consisted of a small hyperpolarizing excursion followed by a larger depolarizing excursion with a time course roughly similar to termination of a single-photon response (n = 4 rods; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on white noise analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Using a white noise voltage stimulus with a smaller standard deviation (0.8 mV), the ETA showed a waveform with a similar shape and time course.
source: Using a white noise voltage stimulus with a smaller standard deviation (0.8 mV), the ETA showed a waveform with a similar shape and time course (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on white noise analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When tested with a small stimulus with 20 Hz cutoff, the ETA appeared as noise, suggesting the rod terminal preferentially responds to slow voltage changes.
source: When we tested a similarly small stimulus but with 20 Hz cutoff, the ETA appeared as noise (Figure 6C), suggesting the rod terminal preferentially responds to slow voltage changes with frequency response characteristics of rods in light and dark, filtering out higher frequency membrane voltage noise.
evidence: This is based on white noise analysis shown in Figure 6C and inference about frequency filtering.

claim: The rod terminal preferentially responds to slow voltage changes with frequency response characteristics of rods in light and dark, filtering out higher frequency membrane voltage noise.
source: When we tested a similarly small stimulus but with 20 Hz cutoff, the ETA appeared as noise (Figure 6C), suggesting the rod terminal preferentially responds to slow voltage changes with frequency response characteristics of rods in light and dark, filtering out higher frequency membrane voltage noise.
evidence: This is inferred from the white noise analysis results.

claim: Transmitter release from rods is very sensitive to small, slow voltage changes similar to those experienced during a single-photon response.
source: These data reinforce the idea that transmitter release from rods is very sensitive to small, slow voltage changes similar to those experienced during a single-photon response, consistent with a role of these multivesicular events in transmitting small light responses at the rod ribbon synapse.
evidence: This is concluded from the white noise analysis results.

claim: For a simulated population of 24 rods, the probability of detecting flashes varied smoothly with flash strength, reaching 75% correct in the 2AFC task between 0.1 and 0.2 Rh*/rod.
source: For a simulated population of 24 rods, the probability of detecting flashes varied smoothly with flash strength, reaching 75% correct in the 2AFC task between 0.1 and 0.2 Rh*/rod (Figure 7J, blue curve).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Flash detection performance compared well to previous measurements of rod-bipolar cell sensitivity, which place their detection threshold (75% correct in the 2AFC task) between 0.1 and 0.3 Rh*/rod.
source: However, flash detection performance compared well to previous measurements of rod-bipolar cell sensitivity, which place their detection threshold (75% correct in the 2AFC task) between 0.1 and 0.3 Rh*/rod (Figure 7J, vertical gray bar) (Field and Rieke, 2002b; Okawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison of model results to published data.

claim: The performance of the simulated rod output with temporally regular multivesicular release falls within the range of flash sensitivities demanded by rod-bipolar cell measurements.
source: Thus, the performance of the simulated rod output with temporally regular multivesicular release falls within the range of flash sensitivities demanded by rod-bipolar cell measurements.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of model and experimental data.

claim: The observed rod vesicle release dynamics can account for rod-bipolar cell flash sensitivity.
source: This indicates that the observed rod vesicle release dynamics can account for rod-bipolar cell flash sensitivity.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results.

claim: The detection threshold was not strongly impacted over a reasonable range of model parameters.
source: In general, the detection threshold was not strongly impacted over a reasonable range of these model parameters: the flash strength generating 75% correct performance was consistent with the detection threshold of rod-bipolar cells (Figure 7J–O, gray bars).
evidence: This is based on parameter sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Each multivesicular event contains ~17 vesicles.
source: Each multivesicular event contains ~17 vesicles.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: With a release rate of ~2 multivesicular events/s, the rod terminal will release ~34 vesicles/s.
source: With a release rate of ~2 multivesicular events/s, this means the rod terminal will release ~34 vesicles/s.
evidence: This is calculated from the event rate and vesicles per event.

claim: The temporally regular multivesicular release model exhibited higher sensitivity than asynchronous Poisson release, given a fixed vesicle budget of 34/s.
source: The temporally regular multivesicular release model exhibited higher sensitivity than asynchronous Poisson release, given a fixed vesicle budget of 34/s.
evidence: This is based on comparative modeling shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The observed statistics of vesicle release from the rod terminal appear to be efficient relative to asynchronous release, given a fixed vesicle budget.
source: Thus, the observed statistics of vesicle release from the rod terminal appear to be efficient relative to asynchronous release, given a fixed vesicle budget.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparative modeling results.

claim: Detection thresholds fell considerably as the Erlang factor increased to four and Erlang factors greater than nine exhibited rapidly diminishing returns on detection thresholds.
source: Examining detection thresholds as a function of the Erlang factor revealed that over a range of multivesicular release rates, detection thresholds fell considerably as the Erlang factor increased to four and Erlang factors greater than nine exhibited rapidly diminishing returns on detection thresholds (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on modeling analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Further increasing the regularity of interevent intervals (increasing the Erlang factor above 9) yields relatively small improvements to the fidelity of transmitting single-photon responses to rod-bipolar cells.
source: Thus, further increasing the regularity of interevent intervals (increasing the Erlang factor above 9) yields relatively small improvements to the fidelity of transmitting single-photon responses to rod-bipolar cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling analysis.

claim: At a membrane potential similar to that in darkness, rods released glutamate-filled vesicles in coordinated multivesicular release events at rates that were not well modeled by Poisson statistics.
source: Using IA(glu) as a presynaptic assay for release, we found that at a membrane potential similar to that in darkness, rods released glutamate-filled vesicles in coordinated multivesicular release events at rates that were not well modeled by Poisson statistics.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Multivesicular events occurred at more regular intervals consistent with an Erlang distribution in which events occurred after waiting 3–12 Poisson intervals.
source: Multivesicular events occurred at more regular intervals consistent with an Erlang distribution in which events occurred after waiting 3–12 Poisson intervals.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of interevent intervals.

claim: Multivesicular release events were extremely sensitive to small voltage changes.
source: Multivesicular release events were also extremely sensitive to small voltage changes.
evidence: This is based on experimental voltage-clamp measurements.

claim: Simulating the impact of these properties on release showed that they can improve the ability of rod-bipolar cells to discriminate suppressed release caused by absorption of a single photon from stochastic pauses in release.
source: Simulating the impact of these properties on release showed that they can improve the ability of rod-bipolar cells to discriminate suppressed release caused by absorption of a single photon from stochastic pauses in release.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and ideal observer analysis.

claim: The ability of the vertebrate visual system to detect single photons arises from high photon capture rates combined with high gain in the phototransduction cascade of rods.
source: The ability of the vertebrate visual system to detect single photons arises from high photon capture rates combined with high gain in the phototransduction cascade of rods.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual system function.

claim: At the synapse from rods to rod-bipolar cell dendrites, there is a non-linear thresholding mechanism in which only responses that exceed a certain size are transmitted.
source: At the synapse from rods to rod-bipolar cell dendrites, there is a non-linear thresholding mechanism in which only responses that exceed a certain size are transmitted, removing baseline noise along with small responses that fall below that threshold (Berntson et al., 2004; Field and Rieke, 2002b; Sampath and Rieke, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mouse retina, 20–35 rods converge onto each rod-bipolar cell.
source: In mouse retina, where 20–35 rods converge onto each rod-bipolar cell (Behrens et al., 2016; Calkins and Sterling, 1999; Rao-Mirotznik et al., 1998; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2013), comparisons between rods and rod-bipolar cells showed thresholds that excluded 40–85% of the single-photon events in rods (Berntson et al., 2004; Field and Rieke, 2002b; Schein and Ahmad, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Comparisons between rods and rod-bipolar cells in mouse retina showed thresholds that excluded 40–85% of the single-photon events in rods.
source: In mouse retina, where 20–35 rods converge onto each rod-bipolar cell (Behrens et al., 2016; Calkins and Sterling, 1999; Rao-Mirotznik et al., 1998; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2013), comparisons between rods and rod-bipolar cells showed thresholds that excluded 40–85% of the single-photon events in rods (Berntson et al., 2004; Field and Rieke, 2002b; Schein and Ahmad, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: In rabbit retina, where 100 rods may converge onto each rod-bipolar cell, as many as 90% of the single-photon responses are removed by the thresholding mechanism.
source: In rabbit retina, where 100 rods may converge onto each rod-bipolar cell, as many as 90% of the single-photon responses are removed by the thresholding mechanism (Trexler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on rabbit retina.

claim: As many as 100,000 rods eventually converge onto a single ganglion cell.
source: Finally, as many as 100,000 rods eventually converge onto a single ganglion cell, allowing the capture of scarce single photons to produce detectable changes in retinal output (Field et al., 2019; Goodchild et al., 1996; Okawa and Sampath, 2007; Takeshita et al., 2017; Taylor and Smith, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: The non-linear thresholding mechanism used at rod-bipolar synapses is thought to occur before summation of rod responses in the rod-bipolar cell soma.
source: The non-linear thresholding mechanism used at rod-bipolar synapses is thought to occur before summation of rod responses in the rod-bipolar cell soma (Field and Rieke, 2002b; Sampath and Rieke, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A key requirement for non-linear thresholding is that glutamate levels in the cleft must be maintained at levels high enough to keep the rod-bipolar cell glutamate receptors saturated.
source: A key requirement for this non-linear thresholding is that glutamate levels in the cleft must be maintained at levels high enough to keep the rod-bipolar cell glutamate receptors saturated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of non-linear thresholding.

claim: By relieving saturation in the receptor signaling cascade, larger reductions in glutamate release have disproportionately larger effects.
source: By relieving saturation in the receptor signaling cascade, larger reductions in glutamate release have disproportionately larger effects (Sampath and Rieke, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Multivesicular release by rods may help ensure that glutamate levels remain high enough at individual synapses to maintain saturation in darkness.
source: In addition to improving regularity, multivesicular release by rods may help ensure that glutamate levels remain high enough at individual synapses to maintain saturation in darkness.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of multivesicular release.

claim: AII amacrine cells show synchronized membrane currents in darkness that arise from synchronous rod inputs into rod-bipolar cells.
source: AII amacrine cells show synchronized membrane currents in darkness that arise from synchronous rod inputs into rod-bipolar cells (Grimes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Two rod-bipolar cell dendrites terminate beneath each rod ribbon in mouse retina.
source: Two rod-bipolar cell dendrites terminate beneath each rod ribbon in mouse retina (Behrens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an anatomical study.

claim: Shared responses of two bipolar cells evoked by large multivesicular release events might contribute to the synchrony among AII amacrine cells.
source: Together with electrical coupling among rods via cones (Jin et al., 2020), shared responses of two such bipolar cells evoked by large multivesicular release events might contribute to the synchrony among AII amacrine cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation combining multiple observations.

claim: Previous recordings of release from mouse rods suggested an overall rate of release at −40 mV of ~11 v/s at 35°C.
source: Our previous recordings of release from a sample of mouse rods suggested an overall rate of release at −40 mV of ~11 v/s at 35°C (Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental measurements.

claim: Assessments of rundown suggest that the true rate in vivo prior to patch rupture may be twice the average rate measured in recordings.
source: However, assessments of rundown in the present study suggest that the true rate in vivo prior to patch rupture may be twice this average rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the rundown analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Earlier computer simulations suggested that, assuming a purely Poisson release process, post-synaptic detection by rod-bipolar cells would require rod release rates of 80–100 v/s.
source: Earlier computer simulations suggested that, assuming a purely Poisson release process, post-synaptic detection by rod-bipolar cells would require rod release rates of 80–100 v/s (Rao et al., 1994; van Rossum and Smith, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: The model indicated that Poisson release at a rate of 34 v/s would not provide the level of performance observed in rod-bipolar cells unless an unusually long suppression duration of 500 ms was employed.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, our model indicated that Poisson release at a rate of 34 v/s would not provide the level of performance observed in rod-bipolar cells unless we employed an unusually long suppression duration of 500 ms.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: At hyperpolarized membrane potentials, glutamate release from rods followed a Poisson distribution similar to that seen at many other neurons.
source: At hyperpolarized membrane potentials, we found that glutamate release from rods followed a Poisson distribution similar to that seen at many other neurons (Malagon et al., 2016; Miki, 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and comparison to literature.

claim: The nearly ubiquitous feature of Poisson release in neurons was established in the 1950s by Bernard Katz who modeled spontaneous release events to develop the quantal hypothesis of neurotransmission.
source: This nearly ubiquitous feature of neurons was established in the 1950s by Bernard Katz who modeled spontaneous release events to develop the quantal hypothesis of neurotransmission (Kavalali, 2015; Kavalali, 2018).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The distribution of intervals between multivesicular events could not be explained by Poisson statistics and were instead more consistent with an Erlang process.
source: However, the dominant feature of release at −40 mV was the appearance of multivesicular release events occurring at fairly regular intervals. The distribution of intervals between multivesicular events could not be explained by Poisson statistics and were instead more consistent with an Erlang process, having a CV narrower than expected from a Poisson process.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: By waiting a specific number of Poisson intervals between each Erlang event, Erlang processes effectively average the underlying Poisson intervals and thereby reduce variability.
source: By waiting a specific number of Poisson intervals between each Erlang event, Erlang processes effectively average the underlying Poisson intervals and thereby reduce variability.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical properties of Erlang processes.

claim: It was suggested previously that an Erlang process might play a role in transmitting single-photon responses from rods.
source: It was suggested previously that an Erlang process might play a role in transmitting single-photon responses from rods (Schein and Ahmad, 2005; Schein and Ahmad, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Experimental data showed a narrower distribution than expected for a Poisson process consistent with the accumulation of as many as 12 Poisson events before each multivesicular release event.
source: Our experimental data showed a narrower distribution than expected for a Poisson process consistent with the accumulation of as many as 12 Poisson events before each multivesicular release event.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The cumulative wait times for replenishment of multiple vesicles to the releasable pool at the base of the synaptic ribbon provides a possible mechanism for achieving an Erlang-like process.
source: The cumulative wait times for replenishment of multiple vesicles to the releasable pool at the base of the synaptic ribbon provides a possible mechanism for achieving an Erlang-like process to enhance regularity in release rates.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Predictions of Schein and Ahmad suggested that achieving reliable single-photon detection with a release rate of 100 v/s/ribbon would require an Erlang process with an Erlang factor of 66.
source: Predictions of Schein and Ahmad suggested that achieving reliable single-photon detection with a release rate of 100 v/s/ribbon would require an Erlang process with an Erlang factor of 66 (i.e., an accumulation of 66 Poisson intervals) (Schein and Ahmad, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous modeling study.

claim: Even a modest increase in regularity combined with multivesicular release can improve the post-synaptic detection of single-photon events.
source: Our model, which among other things differed by including a thresholding non-linearity at the rod-to-rod bipolar cell synapse, showed that even a modest increase in regularity combined with multivesicular release can improve the post-synaptic detection of single-photon events.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The overall rate of release parallels changes in ICa.
source: While the overall rate of release parallels changes in ICa, a small hyperpolarizing voltage change caused appreciable pauses in release.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The average interevent interval dropped close to zero during a simulated single-photon response, rather than declining only ~20–25% as predicted from the decline in ICa.
source: The average interevent interval dropped close to zero during a simulated single-photon response, rather than declining only ~20–25% as predicted from the decline in ICa.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and comparison to expected values.

claim: Recent studies on mice in which synaptic ribbons have been eliminated by deleting the key ribbon protein, Ribeye, showed surprisingly modest deficits.
source: Recent studies on mice in which synaptic ribbons have been eliminated by deleting the key ribbon protein, Ribeye, showed surprisingly modest deficits (Fairless et al., 2020; Okawa et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Multivesicular release in both salamander and mouse rods involves ribbon-associated vesicles.
source: Multivesicular release in both salamander and mouse rods involves ribbon-associated vesicles (Hays et al., 2020a; Hays et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: One role of the ribbon may be to help organize vesicles to promote multivesicular release, implementing an Erlang process to improve the encoding of light responses near scotopic threshold.
source: One role of the ribbon may thus be to help organize vesicles to promote multivesicular release, implementing an Erlang process to improve the encoding of light responses near scotopic threshold (Schein and Ahmad, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of ribbon function.

claim: Rod spherules in mouse retina possess 5800–7500 vesicles apiece.
source: Rod spherules in mouse retina possess 5800–7500 vesicles apiece (Zampighi et al., 2011) and so the entire pool of vesicles would be depleted in roughly a minute if release were maintained at 100 vesicles/s.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an anatomical study.

claim: The entire pool of vesicles in rod spherules would be depleted in roughly a minute if release were maintained at 100 vesicles/s.
source: Rod spherules in mouse retina possess 5800–7500 vesicles apiece (Zampighi et al., 2011) and so the entire pool of vesicles would be depleted in roughly a minute if release were maintained at 100 vesicles/s.
evidence: This is calculated from the vesicle pool size and release rate.

claim: The temporally regular multivesicular release strategy employed by rods provides an efficient means of encoding small voltage changes to meet both constraints on high release rates and requirements for reliable signaling at rod ribbon synapses.
source: Our results suggest that the temporally regular multivesicular release strategy employed by rods provides an efficient means of encoding small voltage changes to meet both constraints on high release rates and requirements for reliable signaling at rod ribbon synapses (Sterling and Laughlin, 2015).
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental and modeling results.
